big_idea: Bigger shapes are made of smaller shapes. 2 triangles can build a square. We compose and decompose.
learning_intention: We are learning to compose and decompose shapes.
student_learning_goal: I can compose and decompose shapes.
success_criteria: I can put smaller shapes together to make a bigger shape.
I can break a bigger shape into smaller shapes.
I can build a 3D structure from solid shapes.
lesson_specific_materials: OPTIONAL: Sammy and Mira — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Lesson 4 compose/decompose tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.hook: Sammy: I have 6 triangles. Can I make a hexagon? Watch — yes!
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Sammy + Mira puppets. 'Friends — yesterday we used position words. Today Sammy shows us COMPOSE and DECOMPOSE.'

Introduce vocabulary. Write COMPOSE and DECOMPOSE on chart. 'Compose = put together. Decompose = break apart.'

Demonstrate compose. Hold up 6 triangle pattern blocks. 'Six triangles. I COMPOSE them — I put them together — and they make a HEXAGON.' Place them on the chart to form a hexagon.

More compose examples:
- 2 triangles compose a square.
- 2 squares compose a rectangle.
- 3 triangles compose a trapezoid.
- 1 triangle + 1 square compose a house shape.

Now demonstrate decompose. 'I take this hexagon. I DECOMPOSE it — I break it apart — and now I have 6 triangles again.'

More decompose examples:
- A square decomposes into 2 triangles.
- A rectangle decomposes into 2 squares.
- A pentagon decomposes into a triangle and a square.

Now 3D. Hold up 4 cubes. 'I COMPOSE 4 cubes — I stack them — and I build a TOWER.' Stack them. 'I can DECOMPOSE the tower back into 4 cubes.'

Real-life examples: 'Lego — you compose pieces to build, decompose to take apart. A puzzle composes from many pieces. Snowflakes decompose when they melt.'

'Sammy says — small shapes can MAKE bigger shapes. Bigger shapes can BREAK into smaller ones. Both ways count.'

Sammy's RULE: 'NAME IT — count SIDES — count CORNERS!' Today: NAME the target — pick the SHAPES — count to check.

Class refrain. Class chants 3x with claps: 'NAME IT — count SIDES — count CORNERS! That's how Sammy hunts!'

'Today we compose and decompose 2D shapes with pattern blocks, then build with 3D shapes.'

steps.instruction: Whole group: compose 4 shapes from pattern blocks. (a) 2 triangles → square. (b) 6 triangles → hexagon. (c) 1 triangle + 1 square → house. (d) 2 trapezoids → hexagon.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say: 'Compose this shape. What blocks do you need?'

steps.instruction: Three stations. Station A: 2D Compose — pair builds 5 target shapes from pattern blocks. Station B: 2D Decompose — pair breaks 5 bigger shapes into smaller ones. Station C: 3D Build — pair stacks 3D models into structures (tower, bridge, house).
Stretch challenge at Station C: build a structure using all 5 different 3D shapes. Describe it.
Discuss the big idea. 'Compose = put TOGETHER. Decompose = take APART. Same shapes, two directions.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Show 6 triangles on chart. Compose into hexagon. Decompose back. Repeat.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the compose/decompose tracker.
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Ask 'Show me compose. Show me decompose.' Mark the tracker.

differentiation.for_emerging: Stay at Station A. Use only 2 triangles → square (one easy target).
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at Station C: 3D structure with all 5 shapes; describe with position words from L3 ('the cone is ABOVE the cylinder, BESIDE the cube').
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide a structured frame: '___ shapes compose a ___.' and 'A ___ decomposes into ___ shapes.'
differentiation.for_movement_learners: NO-PAPER, NO-PURCHASE PATH: skip the printed pattern blocks and the 3D models entirely. Children become the shapes — 2 children compose a SQUARE by holding hands at right angles; 6 children compose a HEXAGON by holding hands in a 6-sided ring; for 3D, 4 children stack as a TOWER (standing in a column) or 5 children form a PYRAMID (4 base + 1 on top of a chair). Whole lesson runs on bodies + classroom space — no purchased pattern blocks, no 3D models.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: composes 2D shapes from pattern blocks; decomposes a bigger shape; builds a 3D structure.

consolidation.exit_routine: Refrain chant 3x. Then each child draws ONE compose: '___ + ___ = ___' (e.g., 'triangle + triangle = square'). Sticky-note the compose and post on the Shape Safari poster.

assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 4 captures A9.4 and A9.5 mastery before the capstone.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child stacks shapes randomly without 'making' a target — repairing the no-target trap at K (Clements, Wilson & Sarama, 2004; Clements & Sarama, 2009; Mulligan & Mitchelmore, 2009)
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
On A9.4/A9.5 shape composition and decomposition, the most-documented K trap is the no-target trap: the child piles pattern blocks or 3D shapes randomly without aiming at a target shape or structure. They lose the 'I am COMPOSING something' frame.

Clements, Wilson & Sarama (2004) traced K-G2 children's shape composition through five levels: Pre-composer (pieces are independent objects, no awareness of part-whole), Picture maker (pieces become parts of pictures but not geometric wholes), Shape composer (deliberately combines shapes to make targeted geometric shapes), Substitution composer (knows two triangles can substitute for a square), Shape composite repeater (uses composites as units). K children typically enter at Pre-composer or Picture maker and the lesson's target is Shape composer — the conceptual move that adds GOAL-DIRECTION to placement.

Clements & Sarama (2009) note that Pre-composers can spend long periods stacking pattern blocks without reaching any geometric target, and that the breakthrough requires explicit teaching of the goal frame: 'pick the target FIRST, then choose the small shapes'. The target card scaffold below operationalises this teaching.

Mulligan & Mitchelmore (2009) on 'awareness of mathematical pattern and structure' (AMPS) show that K children with strong AMPS (who notice and use structure) outperform peers across multiple math domains by Grade 2. Compose-decompose tasks are direct AMPS practice when delivered with target-direction; without target-direction, they are play.

Why this matters: a K child who exits at Pre-composer level treats shape building as decoration, not as a structural activity, and arrives in Grade 1-2 unable to engage with shape decomposition for area, fractions, and geometric reasoning. The repair must happen at K with explicit target naming.

The walkthrough covers the precise moment when a child piles without a target.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station A. Child stacks 5 random blocks. No target in mind. Says 'I made a thing'.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'You built something! Now Sammy asks — what SHAPE were you making?'

If no answer: 'Let's pick a target. We'll compose a HEXAGON. We need 6 triangles. Here they are. Put them together.'

Walk through. 'See — when we COMPOSE, we have a goal. The hexagon is our target. Six triangles compose a hexagon.'

Generalise. 'Sammy says — composing means MAKING a target shape. Pick the target FIRST, then choose the small shapes.'

Now practice. Pick a square as target. 'What 2 shapes compose a square? (Two triangles.) Put them together.'

If still piling: provide a target card. 'Match the picture. Compose THIS.' Force the goal-directed behaviour.

Long-term recovery: every compose activity starts with naming the target.
expected_student_responses: (Strong) Names target, picks shapes, composes independently.
(Stretched) Composes the same target two different ways.
common_misconceptions: Composing means stacking. (Repair: composing means making a TARGET shape.)
Any pile of shapes is composing. (Repair: composing has a goal.)
Decompose means destroy. (Repair: decompose means break into the SMALLER shapes that compose it.)
recovery_moves: DIAGNOSTIC A — child piles without a target (Clements/Wilson/Sarama 2004 Pre-composer level): provide a target card showing the goal shape (a printed hexagon outline, a printed house). Child must MATCH their build to the picture. Force the goal frame. Repeat for the next 3 builds before letting them choose their own target.

DIAGNOSTIC B — child names the target but cannot pick the right small shapes (Picture-maker level — pieces are visual decoration, not geometric parts): walk them through the part-count. 'A hexagon needs SIX triangles. Count out six.' Then place one triangle at a time, naming each. The explicit part-count is the bridge to Shape-composer level.

DIAGNOSTIC C — child composes one way and stops (no AMPS / structure awareness, Mulligan & Mitchelmore 2009): challenge with substitution. 'You made a hexagon with 6 triangles. Now make the SAME hexagon with 2 trapezoids.' Or: 'You made a square with 2 triangles. Can you make a square with 4 smaller triangles?' Multiple compositions for the same target = Substitution composer level.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of A9.4 (compose/decompose 2D) and A9.5 (build 3D).

parts_outline.task: Compose: draw the smaller shapes that make 4 target shapes (square, hexagon, rectangle, house).
Decompose: draw the smaller shapes inside 3 bigger shapes.
Draw a 3D structure you built. Label the shapes you used.
